newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Security men need "eyes everywhere" in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Security men need "eyes everywhere" in Hong Kong.

text.p: From frogmen bobbing in one of the world's most polluted harbours to undercover bodyguards in luxury hotel rooms, Hong Kong is staging its biggest ever security operation for next week's handover celebrations.
The threat of snipers, missiles and bombs, as well as unruly crowds, are the devil's brew that security planners say they have to contend with.
In the last five days before Hong Kong returns to China, an ever tighter cordon is being drawn around the sprawling convention centre which is the site of next Monday's end-of-empire ceremony.

Led by Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Britain's heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles, about 60 foreign dignitaries are due to descend on the colony in the coming days to join several thousand Hong Kong VIPs.
New British Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright are among the group.
"Now we just pray," a senior Hong Kong police officer said on Thursday.
The operation extends from the waters of Hong Kong harbour to the territory's teeming high-rise buildings, making it one of the most complex staged in Asia.
Marine police plan to devote one-quarter of their fleet of 100 vessels solely to the handover arrangements, including craft not normally used for patrol duties, such as training ships.
Frogmen have been making daily inspections of waters that the flying-saucer-like convention centre overlooks.
A 100-metre (100-yard) offshore exclusion zone has been established along the shore where the celebration takes place in central Hong Kong.
The zone covers the royal yacht Britannia where Prince Charles will stay during his three days in Hong Kong from this Saturday.
On shore, there are even more elaborate plans -- and challenges.

A key planner of the land-based operation said density of population, Hong Kong's numerous high-rise buildings and lack of experience in dealing with large-scale international gatherings were the key issues that needed to be overcome.

"Density of population is our nightmare," he said. "When the Pope goes to Poland you put him in a green field and surround it with police. You can't do that here. There's not a big enough green field."
The officer, who asked not be identified, said security in Hong Kong was more complex than in all other major world cities because it was a "three-dimensional" problem.
"With all the high rise buildings you have to look up, down and sideways," he said. "You have to have eyes everywhere."
